title: Washington Sanctions the ICC, Buys Diesel From Moscow and Weighs a Third War as the Houthis Bring the Fight to Riyadh
subhead: The US moved this week to dismantle the International Criminal Court, cut a diesel deal that funds Russia's war while calling for a new president in Kyiv, and edge toward joining the Yemen campaign after a mass-casualty Houthi strike on Saudi Arabia's main airport. Oil whipped between $88 and $104 as the G7 burned through emergency reserves, and Asia's naval order shifted as Japan and South Korea opened the door to nuclear-powered submarines.

sections.heading: The ICC Became a Battlefield — and the Prize Went to Its Former Judge
sections.body:
The week's most consequential move came on Friday, when Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced sweeping US sanctions on the International Criminal Court itself, not merely individual judges and prosecutors as in earlier rounds, per Al Jazeera and Reuters. Rubio said Washington would 'ban transactions with this rogue court', freeze ICC assets held in US territory and penalise companies servicing the court, giving US firms a six-month grace period to wind down business. It was a full-frontal attempt to defund and demolish a Hague institution built in 2002 to prosecute war crimes, genocide and crimes against humanity.

The timing was pointed to the hour. The measures landed just after South African jurist Navanethem 'Navi' Pillay, a former ICC judge now sitting on the International Court of Justice, was awarded the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize, with the Norwegian committee explicitly choosing her as a show of support for institutions under attack, warning that international law is 'under tremendous pressure' and that 'peace requires justice'. Rubio's framing was blunt: 'Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC', pledging to dismantle it 'brick by brick'.

The trigger is the court's 2024 arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former defence minister Yoav Gallant over suspected Gaza war crimes, plus an earlier US probe into Afghanistan. Neither the US nor Israel is a party to the Rome Statute — but the court can still prosecute their citizens for abuses on member states' territory. The move converts a legal dispute into a live alliance fault line: European states, Canada, Japan and the UN have already rallied to the court, and the week ends with the transatlantic partners on opposite sides of an institution they jointly fund.
sections.whyItMatters: Washington is now openly trying to dismantle a Hague court its own NATO allies fund and back. That makes international accountability bodies a targetable instrument of great-power conflict and forces Europe to decide whether to shield the court — a decision that will define the alliance's legal and moral posture for years.

sections.heading: The Houthis Hit Riyadh's Airport Three Times, and Washington Edges Toward a Third War
sections.body:
The Red Sea war widened dramatically this week. On October 8, Houthi attacks on two Saudi airports killed at least three and injured 36, with one target being King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh — the kingdom's main gateway. Saudi-led coalition forces struck back, claiming 82 Houthi military targets destroyed. By October 10, the Houthis had hit the same airport again, and issued a 'last warning to global airlines' over Saudi airspace, a direct threat to civil aviation rather than just shipping. Then on October 11, a missile and drone attack on the airport killed at least 12 people and wounded more than 300, including four Saudis, eight foreigners and one American, per AP and Reuters. It was the third strike on Saudi airport infrastructure in a week.

The escalation forced Washington up the ladder. Trump condemned the attack as 'terrible' and said the US is evaluating whether to join Saudi Arabia's retaliatory strikes on the Houthis, with plans to call Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman. A Saudi-led air campaign is already under way, and Pakistan has joined the air campaign — extending, not closing, the Mecca Pact alignment building since August. Analysts quoted by the South China Morning Post warned the offensive risks pulling Riyadh into direct war with Tehran.

This all unfolded against the Yemen government's own offensive. On October 5, Presidential Leadership Council chairman Rashad al-Alimi announced a nationwide campaign involving roughly 100,000 troops aimed at Houthi territory and the Bab el-Mandab Strait. By October 6, government forces said they had retaken the Red Sea port city of Mocha and positions around the strait after more than 1,000 strikes, only for the Houthis to claim strikes on Riyadh's airport and encircle Taiz. Turkey and Pakistan agreed at an emergency Riyadh meeting to send forces to Saudi Arabia under the Mecca Pact, giving the August agreement its first concrete military dimension.
sections.whyItMatters: A mass-casualty strike on the Saudi capital's main airport forces Riyadh and Washington up the escalation ladder at the exact moment the US is deciding whether to re-enter the Iran war. With Hormuz already contested, Bab el-Mandab is becoming the next chokepoint, and the US risk of being drawn into a third simultaneous front has risen sharply.

sections.heading: Washington Buys Diesel From Moscow While Calling for a New President in Kyiv
sections.body:
The Ukraine track produced the week's sharpest contradiction. As envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner gathered with Ukrainian and European officials in Miami to pitch a 'new' peace plan, the Trump administration cut a deal easing restrictions on Russian diesel exports — a move Ukraine publicly labelled a 'gift' to Russia. Under the arrangement, Russia would supply 300,000 tonnes of diesel immediately, followed by a further 1.5 million tonnes, per Al Jazeera. Axios reported a US official saying the deal was cut because Zelensky had ignored earlier US requests.

Trump then went further, saying Ukraine 'should get a new president' who would agree to end the war, suggesting Zelensky 'has not done enough' — comments tied to Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian refineries, which he blames for high US diesel prices before the midterms. Zelensky told Axios the arrangement is 'not fair and not honest', and GOP lawmakers rejected it outright. Putin, meanwhile, told Trump that immediate talks are unlikely, blaming continued Ukrainian drone strikes — undercutting the 'productive' language US officials used about Miami.

The battlefield refused to cooperate. Ukraine fired roughly 650 drones at the Moscow region overnight on October 6, one of the war's largest single waves on the Russian capital, hitting the Kapotnya refinery and paralysing Moscow-area airports. Ukraine also struck a sanctioned shadow-fleet tanker, the Aframax Rio, off Sochi, setting it ablaze and rescuing all 23 crew, extending the Black Sea war to Russia's sanctions-evasion shipping. Russia's response was its deadliest night in weeks: 28 killed across Ukraine on October 8, including five children and three 12-month-old infants, with 20 killed when a missile hit a Pryluky apartment block.
sections.whyItMatters: Trump is publicly calling for regime change in Kyiv while buying diesel from Moscow — an inversion that weakens Ukraine's leverage and hands Putin a sanctions-revenue lifeline at the moment Washington claims to be brokering peace. It also exposes a deepening split with Congress and European allies over Russia policy, even as strikes on Ukraine's energy grid presage a hard winter.

sections.heading: Iran Keeps Hormuz Hostage as the G7 Burns Through Emergency Reserves
sections.body:
Energy dominated the week's price action. The G7 agreed on October 5 to release up to 100 million barrels of oil and diesel over four months — a front-loaded diesel release in 20 days — after a Trump threat to ban US diesel exports, a direct hit at the EU and UK before winter. Trump later said 'we were never going to do it', framing the threat as leverage. France added 10 million barrels of its own diesel, and the IEA agreed to accelerate stock releases.

But the barrels kept getting attacked. On October 7, the IRGC attacked four tankers in or near the Strait of Hormuz and threatened a fifth, even as Gulf oil flows climbed. By October 10, UKMTO had recorded eleven attacks on vessels in the first week of October, ten in the strait, described as a wartime high. Rubio claimed Iran has 'lost complete control' of the strait, while Tehran said tankers hit mines in the southern lane — a discrepancy that matters, because deliberate mining is coercion while uncontrolled attacks risk accidental escalation with Gulf states. Iran kept the strait closed until seven conditions are met and, per Iran International, sees the gap between talks and war narrowing.

Prices whipsawed on the conflicting signals. Brent dipped below $100 on October 5, fell back below $90 on October 6 as WTI traded near $88.60, then topped $104 on October 9 as a Gulf hurricane collided with strike fears, before pulling back after Trump ruled out US strikes on Iran before the November 3 midterms. Tehran signalled it is ready for a prolonged war, and the Soufan Center noted both sides appear to be preparing for renewed combat after the vote. The pause, in other words, is political — not strategic.
sections.whyItMatters: The market is pricing calm that the physical strait does not support. Emergency reserves are being drained faster than they are refilled while Iran demonstrates it can tax every barrel shipped through Hormuz. The post-election window is where escalation risk now concentrates, with the US buffer of strategic stocks thinner than it was a week ago.

sections.heading: Japan and South Korea Move Toward Nuclear Submarines as Lithuania Scraps Its Nuclear Ban
sections.body:
A nuclear threshold moved quietly this week. Japan's government is weighing whether to mention nuclear-powered submarines in the three national security documents it plans to revise by year's end — the first time Tokyo would formally open the door to a technology it has never fielded, per Kyodo, Jiji Press and the Yomiuri Shimbun. The proposed language is soft, listing the capability as an option worth studying rather than a procurement decision, but it tests the boundaries of Japan's Atomic Energy Basic Law and its post-war restraints under PM Sanae Takaichi. South Korea, meanwhile, is moving toward nuclear-powered submarines too, having secured US approval to pursue the capability alongside its new 3,000-ton indigenous boat.

On NATO's eastern flank, Lithuania's parliament backed the first reading of a constitutional amendment to remove its ban on nuclear weapons, a step toward potentially hosting allied nuclear arms. The vote followed Trump's suggestion he is considering a permanent US base in Lithuania, which Lithuanian officials said they would help fund. The Kremlin responded sharply through Dmitry Peskov, who said Russia would be forced to retaliate if nuclear weapons are deployed there. NATO answered with its annual Steadfast Noon nuclear exercise — initially over Italian airspace — held despite Russian signalling, days after Putin's warning over Kaliningrad, and France test-launched its next-generation M51.3 submarine-launched ballistic missile.

In parallel, NATO sent all 32 member countries' military chiefs to Kyiv for the first time, with the Military Committee meeting on air defence and hybrid warfare, and the Ankara summit focusing on defence manufacturing. A Stars and Stripes report warned Russia's 'shadow war' of sabotage has NATO on the defensive. Rubio insisted US pressure on allies to raise defence spending is 'not hostile'.
sections.whyItMatters: Nuclear propulsion and nuclear sharing are threshold capabilities that break decades of restraint. If Japan and South Korea both move toward nuclear-powered submarines, Northeast Asia's undersea balance shifts and China's ability to operate freely in the Pacific narrows — while nuclear sharing on the Baltic hardens Europe's divide and gives Moscow a concrete grievance to act on.

sections.heading: China Opens a Third Overseas Base, Squeezes Taiwan and Signals Only a 'Mini Stimulus'
sections.body:
Beijing expanded its military footprint and its pressure on Taipei in the same week. The PLA opened the China-Laos Military Joint Support and Training Center at Ban Keun — its third overseas facility after Djibouti and Cambodia, and its first oriented around air power, with a runway up to 6,562 feet, about 40 miles north of Vientiane. ISW tied it to Laos's deep dependence on Beijing, including $10.5 billion of debt, roughly 82 percent of Laotian GDP. In response, the US Marine Corps prepared to fire anti-ship weaponry on a remote Japanese island near Taiwan, and Japan and the US readied the Keen Sword 2026 drills around the southwest island chain. Taiwan tracked 16 Chinese ships around the island and logged continued PLA joint combat-readiness patrols, while North Korea's state media defended Beijing's 'One China' policy and Kim Jong Un pledged continued support for Russia's war.

Taiwan read the blockade risk as imminent, planning to spend roughly US$850 million to replenish ammunition stocks, per the South China Morning Post, with troops on outlying islands preparing for a possible first strike. RAND noted China is exploring 'cognitive' warfare effects, and ACLED called China's maritime presence around the island the new normal. China's economic answer was minimal: a 'mini stimulus', in Bloomberg's words, sufficient to secure the GDP target but 'not much more', with Reuters noting Beijing acknowledged 'prominent' imbalances.
sections.whyItMatters: Beijing is running two clocks at once — a slow-burn military squeeze on Taiwan and a deliberately calibrated, minimal stimulus. Taiwan's munitions buyout shows Taipei believes a blockade is a live, near-term risk, while China's reluctance to spend big suggests it is preserving fiscal room for a longer confrontation rather than buying near-term growth.

sections.heading: Washington Reverses Course on Myanmar and Turns Venezuelan Oil Into a US Instrument
sections.body:
The week also showed Washington reassembling its non-European relationships around supply chains and raw leverage. The Trump administration opened direct talks with Myanmar's military junta, reversing years of isolation of the generals who seized power in the 2021 coup, per Reuters. The outreach — led in part by Assistant Secretary of State Michael Vance — focused first on shutting down scam centres targeting Americans, and separately on rare earths, per Mining.com.au.

In the Americas, the administration continued folding Venezuela's oil sector into its hemispheric strategy after the operation against Nicolás Maduro, publicly highlighting a subsequent oil deal while PolitiFact flagged an inflated figure for the gains. A Venezuelan oilman under an overseas arrest warrant is now a key broker for the administration, and GIS Reports framed the 'Donroe' doctrine as a bid to push China out of the Americas. The dispute over Guyana's oil wealth remains live alongside the Venezuela file.

Rubio, on a NATO tour through Iceland, Greece and Portugal, used a speech beneath the Acropolis in Athens to urge Western nations to reclaim their 'civilisational roots', framing nationalism and alliances as complementary — the clearest articulation yet of how Washington wants to reconcile its America-first doctrine with its alliance commitments. In Brazil, student-led protests followed Flavio Bolsonaro topping the first round of the presidential election, and the African Union launched the continent's first credit rating agency, an alternative to Western agencies.
sections.whyItMatters: Engaging a sanctioned junta over rare earths and converting an arrest campaign into direct control of Venezuelan crude shows Washington prioritising supply-chain security and hemispheric energy leverage over its democracy-and-sanctions posture. Both moves put Beijing's access to critical minerals and Latin American oil directly on the negotiating table.

sections.heading: The Gaza Ceasefire Turns One With the Fighting Unstopped
sections.body:
On the anniversary of the US-brokered Gaza ceasefire, Israeli attacks continued to kill Palestinians, including a child among eight killed on the anniversary day itself, per Al Jazeera. Hundreds of doctors demanded the World Medical Association suspend Israel, and mass pro-Palestinian marches were held in London, Rome and Berlin. Israel's economy, Al Jazeera noted, has prospered through years of war even as prices worry voters. The ceasefire remains stalled over the disarmament of Hamas, with a scaled-down but ongoing Israeli campaign a year into the truce.

The Lebanon track stayed live too, with an Israeli drone attack wounding six near the Syrian border — testing the trilateral Israel-Lebanon framework signed in June. The two tracks are now linked by the same disarmament question: without progress on Hamas disarmament, Israel has little incentive to restrain operations in Lebanon, keeping a second front warm while the Hormuz crisis occupies Washington. And the Gaza file sits directly behind Friday's ICC sanctions — the arrest warrants for Netanyahu and Gallant that triggered Washington's campaign against the court remain the permanent fault line in Western politics.
sections.whyItMatters: A ceasefire that is nominally a year old but still produces daily casualties undermines the credibility of US-brokered frameworks at the very moment Washington is trying to extend its writ from Yemen to Iran. It also keeps Gaza — and the ICC warrants it generated — as the through-line connecting the court sanctions, the Israeli election on October 27 and the wider Middle East escalation.

bottomLine: This was the week Washington stopped pretending its wars were separate problems and started treating every institution between them as a battlefield. It sanctioned the entire ICC hours after a former ICC judge won the Nobel Peace Prize, cutting itself off from the European allies who fund the court. It bought diesel from Moscow while calling for a new president in Kyiv, handing Putin revenue and leverage at the exact moment it claimed to be brokering peace. And after a Houthi strike killed 12 at Riyadh's main airport, it edged toward joining a third simultaneous war — in Yemen — even as it froze strikes on Iran only until the November 3 midterms. Meanwhile the physical buffers are thinning: the G7 is draining emergency oil reserves while Iran keeps attacking tankers in Hormuz, NATO ran a nuclear exercise against Russian nuclear signalling, and Japan, South Korea and Lithuania each moved toward nuclear thresholds that were closed a month ago. The through-line is political timing: Washington is buying calm before its own midterms while adversaries, allies and institutions alike reposition for what comes after. The post-election window — from Hormuz to Kyiv to a possible US role in Yemen — is where the next escalation is already loaded, and every actor is behaving as if it knows it.
